sweep_summary: Izon (izon1238) is not in the catalog. The single title-match item, Efere 1981 'Pitch accent in the Bumo and Nembe dialects of Ijo', is a BA long essay from the University of Port Harcourt (Glottolog 41521; Bumo = Izon, Nembe = Southeast Ijo); it is about accent placement in this language but no copy exists online, and it is presumably superseded by Efere's 1994 thesis / 2001 UBC Working Papers monograph 'The pitch system of the Bumo dialect of Izon' (pp. Crossref located Williamson 1988 'Tone and Accent in Ịjọ' (Foris, DOI 10.1515/9783110874266.253), paywalled behind a De Gruyter robot check, and the Ijaw-languages Wikipedia bibliography lists Williamson 1978 'From tone to pitch accent: the case of Ịjọ' (Kiabàrà). No first-hand stress/accent statement was read; all evidence points to Izon being described as a pitch accent (restricted tone) system, but that is inferred from titles only. Highest acquisition priorities: Efere 2001 (UBCWPL 4) and Williamson 1988. Saved:, glottolog_izon1238_refs.bib, }.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kolokuma Izon is a two-tone (H/L) language in which stress is non-contrastive and fully predictable from the tone pattern: stress falls on the first high tone of a run of high tones, on the first half of a phonetic falling tone, on the first half of a phonetic rising tone (except that when the first vowel is high and the second non-high the second half is stressed), and on the first syllable of a VV unit. Rhythm is described as neither syllable-timed nor stress-timed; tone groups occupy roughly equal time intervals.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; snippet queries for 'secondary stress' inside the book return nothing.
new_statements.exceptions: Rule (c) has a segmental exception: in a rising tone whose first vowel is high and second vowel non-high, stress moves to the second part (ndaá 'but', anjá 'so, then').
new_statements.domain_note: Examples are single words (bird, sweat, 'but', 'so, then', an interrogative emphasizer), but the rules refer to phonetic tone sequences, which in Kolokuma are set at the level of the tone group/breath group (the passage follows the intonation section, and the preceding snippet text is about breath groups ending in low tones); stress is thus a phrase-level correlate of the tonal melody rather than a lexical word property. Source describes the Kolokuma dialect (kolo1262) only; Jenewari 1989 notes that Kolokuma and Mein are two-tone while Nembe and many Southern Izon dialects (Bumo, Arogbo) are 'accent' systems with one basic high per phrase, so this statement should not be extended to Bumo or other Izon dialects without Efere 2001.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes the Kolokuma dialect of Izon (Glottolog dialect kolo1262 'Kolokuma-Opokuma', under izon1238), a two-tone (H/L) dialect. Other Izon dialects (Bumo bumo1235, Arogbo) are described by Jenewari 1989 and Efere 2001 as pitch accent systems with one basic high per phrase; the Kolokuma stress-from-tone rule should be tagged as dialect-specific. The secondary Ndimele & Efere snippet ('Bumo.. is essentially pitch accent') refers to bumo1235.

new_statements.quote: Nembe and Bumo are pitch-accent systems (Bumo perhaps more so) in the usual typology. In Nembe, for instance, a few words have two underlying Hs, e.g. óporópo 'pig' and álalánda 'orange'; while in Bumo, words have at most one underlying H. Williamson (1978) argues that Proto-Ijo was a tonal system, and that the trend, as in the Bantu languages, is that the Ijo lects are drifting toward a pitch-accent system. [...] culminative in function; that is, it serves to mark one syllable per word as being prominent. There are, however, many differences among the stress languages. A stress language may be free or fixed. In a language with free stress, prominence may be placed on any syllable in the word. [...] 2.3.4 SYSTEMS COMBINING TONE AND STRESS Van der Hulst and Smith (1988) list some languages in which both tone and stress co-occur.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Efere classes the Bumo dialect as a pitch accent system: each word has at most one underlying H (accent), which is culminative (one prominent syllable per word); accent placement is lexical (four word classes A-D per Hyman's summary of Efere 2001: 158-159, class A having no accent) and is not stated in terms of a fixed syllable position. The snippets discuss 'stress' only as a typological notion (free vs fixed stress; systems combining tone and stress) and do not assign Bumo a phonetic word-stress rule.

new_statements.exceptions: Contrast with Nembe, where a few words carry two underlying Hs (óporópo 'pig', álalánda 'orange'); an unaccented prefix V is extratonal and gets a default low (4.1.8). new_statements.rule_in_words: Kolokuma Izon has two tonemes (high and low, 1.6.1) and a predictable, non-contrastive stress that is read off the tone pattern: stress falls on the first syllable of a run of high tones, on the first half of a falling tone, on the first half of a rising tone (except that when the first vowel is high and the second non-high the second half is stressed), and on the first syllable of a VV emphasizer unit. Rhythm is described as neither stress-timed nor syllable-timed, with tone groups roughly isochronous.

new_statements.exceptions: Rule (c) exception: in a rising tone whose first vowel is high and second non-high, the second part is stressed (ndaá 'but', anjá 'so, then'). p. 29: question intonation adds 'a raising of all high tones and extra stress on stressed syllables'. p. 109: English loans are assigned to tone classes 'in which the stressed syllable is interpreted as high tone'.
new_statements.identity_note: Williamson 1965 = Kolokuma dialect (Kolokuma-Opokuma clan, River Nun; Glottolog kolo1262 under izon1238), with Kalabari as the comparison dialect. Efere 2001 and Efere 1981 = Bumo dialect (Bayelsa State; Glottolog bumo1235 under izon1238), Efere 1981 also covering Nembe (= Southeast Ijo, ijs / a different Glottolog language). WALS 'Ijo (Kolokuma)' = izon1238 with Williamson 1965 as source.

readall_conflicts: No two sources disagree about the same variety. Williamson 1965 describes Kolokuma as a two-tone language with fully predictable, tone-driven stress (first of a run of high tones, etc.). Efere 2001 describes Bumo as a pitch accent system with at most one underlying H per word and gives no phonetic stress rule; Efere himself frames this as a dialect split inside Izon (Kolokuma and Kalabari tonal, Nembe and Bumo pitch accent, following Williamson 1978 on a drift from tone to pitch accent). Secondary sources seen in snippets agree with that split (Jenewari 1989: Kolokuma and Mein two tones without downstep, Bumo and Arogbo one basic high tone per phrase; Hyman 2018 on Efere's four Bumo word classes A-D, class A unaccented). So the catalog's dialect-unspecified 'Izon' record rests on Kolokuma; a Bumo entry would read pitch accent.
